venues.a: Avenida da Liberdade / Marquês de Pombal
venues.d: The capital's defining grand hotel — a 1950s palace of Louis XVI and Art Deco rooms, above the city on the edge of the Liberdade.
A restored 16th-century palace on the Liberdade — gardens, a rooftop pool and quiet grandeur in the city's most exclusive quarter.
An 18th-century house on Praça Luís de Camões, restored by Pritzker laureate Eduardo Souto de Moura — the cultural heart of the city.
A 15th-century palace woven into the oldest quarter, below São Jorge Castle — intimate, characterful, deeply Lisbon.
A design-forward 15-room townhouse in a leafy residential quarter — wellness-led, private and quietly indulgent.

venues.n: Pousada de Lisboa, Praça do Comércio
venues.d: A former royal ministry on the grand riverfront square — heritage rooms opening straight onto the Tagus and the Baixa.
A restored baroque palace by the architect of Mafra's basilica — a wine-led house of real character above the old town.
A polished, design-led house on the seam of Baixa and Chiado — art-forward and impeccably placed for the historic centre.
A well-run boutique house in the heart of the Baixa grid — quietly stylish and steps from Rossio and the river.
José Avillez's theatre of contemporary Portuguese cooking — the country's most celebrated table, and one of the world's finest.
Henrique Sá Pessoa's two-star room — Portuguese produce with an Asian hand, precise and generous in equal measure.
José Avillez's all-vegetable fine-dining room beside Belcanto — a starred, sustainability-led ode to Portuguese produce.
Pedro Pena Bastos's minimalist, produce-led cooking inside the Ritz — refined, seasonal, quietly confident.
Alexandre Silva's open-kitchen counter beside the Basílica da Estrela — sixteen surprising 'moments' of new Portuguese cooking.
Vincent Farges's pared-back room above the river — French precision and Portuguese produce, with one of the city's best views.
A refined, ingredient-led kitchen on the Belém waterfront — elegant Portuguese cooking beside the great monuments.
Japanese-Mediterranean cooking of real finesse — the Madrid group's Lisbon star, all clean lines and precise fish.
Paulo Morais's eight-seat kaiseki counter — Lisbon's most serious, meticulous Japanese room.

venues.a: Parque das Nações (Vasco da Gama Tower)
venues.d: Rui Silvestre's cooking at the top of Lisbon's tallest tower — a glass room over the river and the 25 de Abril skyline.
Joachim Koerper's long-held star above the Edward VII Park — classical technique and a commanding view down to the river.
João Sá's personal, well-travelled cooking — Portuguese roots threaded with Indian, African, Brazilian and Thai notes.
Ljubomir Stanisic's spirited tasting menu in the Bairro Alto — bold, narrative cooking with a dedicated vegetarian menu.
Marlene Vieira's first star — assured, contemporary Portuguese cooking from one of the country's most respected chefs.
A fourteen-seat, fourteen-course counter — intimate, precise cooking and one of Lisbon's newest stars.
A wine-led star with a seasonal tasting menu — cooking built around an exceptional cellar.
João Rodrigues's neighbourhood bistro on the edge of Belém — simple, superb Portuguese produce, made for sharing.
A snout-to-tail ode to Portuguese pork — crackling, croquettes and the famed bifana, done with real craft.
A warm Alentejo tavern around a U-shaped counter — wholesome petiscos and duck rice, shared shoulder to shoulder.
An unconventional gastrobar — a modern tasco built for sharing plates in a laid-back room.

venues.a: Cais do Sodré (Time Out Market area)
venues.d: Marlene Vieira's playful gastrobar — classic Portuguese dishes given a daring, contemporary turn.
Lisbon's great seafood institution since the 1950s — prawns, spider crab, oysters and the famous prego, in cheerful chaos.

The masterpiece of Portugal's Manueline style, built with the wealth of the sea route to India that Vasco da Gama opened — his tomb lies just inside the door. The vast cloister, all carved rope, coral and armillary spheres, rewards a slow, unhurried walk; go early or book a timed entry to be ahead of the coaches. A logical first stop, and steps from the custard tarts.

venues.n: Belém Tower (Torre de Belém / Torre de São Vicente)
venues.d: The little limestone fortress standing in the Tagus was the ceremonial gateway from which the great voyages of discovery set out, and it remains the postcard image of Lisbon. The Manueline carving — rope motifs, a stone rhinoceros — is best seen from the riverside walk; the interior is cramped, so many families simply admire it from the promenade at golden hour.

The original pastel de nata, made from a convent recipe bought in 1837 and still kept secret in the 'Oficina do Segredo'. They sell over 20,000 a day; skip the takeaway queue and be seated in the warren of blue-tiled back rooms, where warm tarts arrive dusted with cinnamon. An easy, universally loved treat for all generations.

venues.n: Padrão dos Descobrimentos (Monument to the Discoveries)
venues.d: A 52-metre stone caravel surging toward the Atlantic, its prow led by Henry the Navigator and a procession of the explorers, kings and cartographers of Portugal's golden age. Take the lift to the rooftop terrace for a clean panorama over Belém, the river and the great compass-rose pavement laid out below.

venues.n: MAAT — Museum of Art, Architecture and Technology
venues.d: Amanda Levete's sculptural white wave on the riverbank, clad in 15,000 three-dimensional tiles that shimmer with reflected water — you can walk right up over its roof for a low, sweeping river view. Inside, changing contemporary shows pair with the handsome old Central Tejo power station next door. A calm, design-led counterpoint to Belém's monuments.

venues.n: São Jorge Castle (Castelo de São Jorge)
venues.d: A Moorish citadel taken by Portugal's first king in 1147, crowning the highest of Lisbon's hills with the single finest panorama of the city, the Tagus and the 25 de Abril Bridge. Peacocks wander the ramparts and an archaeological site layers Iron Age, Moorish and medieval remains. Consider a private guide and a taxi up the steep lanes for older travellers.

The oldest, most atmospheric quarter — a maze of stepped alleys, laundry lines and tiled façades that survived the 1755 earthquake — and the birthplace of fado, Portugal's soulful song of longing. A discreet advisor can reserve an intimate fado house for a private, unhurried dinner rather than the tourist floor shows.

Set in a former water-pumping station at the heart of Alfama, this is the place to understand fado before you hear it live — recordings, guitars, and the stories of legendary voices like Amália Rodrigues. Compact and well-curated, with a free audio guide; a good, cool hour when the hills tire the legs.

The most photographed terrace in Lisbon — a tiled pergola draped in bougainvillea framing the tumble of Alfama's terracotta roofs down to the river and the white dome of the National Pantheon. Come early morning to have the balustrade almost to yourself; a bench here is one of the city's great free pleasures.

venues.n: Praça do Comércio & Rua Augusta Arch
venues.d: Lisbon's grand riverfront square, once the site of the royal palace lost to the 1755 earthquake and now a vast open forecourt opening onto the Tagus. Walk beneath the triumphal Rua Augusta Arch — you can climb it for a view straight down the grid — into the Pombaline downtown. Flat, easy walking and full of cafés for a multi-generation group.

The dead-straight grid rebuilt by the Marquis of Pombal after 1755, using the world's first purpose-built anti-seismic 'gaiola' timber frames — a landmark of Enlightenment urban planning you walk through without noticing the engineering. Pedestrian Rua Augusta, mosaic pavements and elegant shopfronts make it the natural spine of a first day.

A wrought-iron neo-Gothic lift from 1902, a cousin in spirit to Eiffel's Paris, that hoists you from the flat Baixa up to the ruined Carmo Convent and a small rooftop viewing deck. Queues can be long; a savvier route is to reach the top platform from the Carmo side and skip the wait entirely.

venues.n: Carmo Convent & Archaeological Museum (Convento do Carmo)
venues.d: The roofless Gothic nave left open to the sky by the 1755 earthquake — its bare stone arches are the most haunting, quietly moving space in the city, and a small museum of oddments (mummies, tombs, tiles) sits in the chancel. Rarely crowded, and deeply atmospheric for anyone who cares about history.

Chiado is Lisbon's most elegant quarter — grand cafés, bookshops, jewellers and the storied A Brasileira with Pessoa's bronze at a pavement table — flowing uphill into bohemian Bairro Alto, sleepy by day and alive by night. The daytime browse suits a refined, unhurried afternoon; the nightlife is best sampled selectively.

The vintage 1930s 'Remodelado' tram that clatters through Alfama, Graça, Baixa and Estrela, threading lanes too steep and narrow for anything modern — history and scenery in one 45-minute ride. It gets packed; board early at Martim Moniz or Campo de Ourique, or charter a private vintage tram for the family to ride in comfort.

One of the world's great private collections in a single elegant building set in serene modernist gardens — Egyptian antiquities, Islamic and East Asian art, Rembrandt and Monet, and a peerless room of René Lalique jewellery. Calm, world-class and never overwhelming; the garden café is a lovely veg-friendly pause. (Note: the founder's collection has been in phased renovation — confirm current opening.)

venues.n: National Tile Museum (Museu Nacional do Azulejo)
venues.d: Set in the golden-and-tiled Madre de Deus convent, this holds five centuries of the azulejo tilework that defines Portugal — the highlight a 23-metre panorama of Lisbon as it looked before the 1755 earthquake. A little out of the centre and all the quieter for it; the convent church alone is worth the taxi.

A plain façade hiding one of Europe's most sumptuous interiors — its Chapel of St John the Baptist was built in Rome from lapis lazuli, ivory, gold and silver, blessed by the Pope, then shipped to Lisbon. One of the few buildings to survive 1755 intact; ten quiet minutes that leave visitors stunned.

A gleaming late-Baroque and neoclassical basilica of grey-and-cream marble, its great dome a landmark on the skyline, built by Queen Maria I in thanks for the birth of an heir. Climb to the roof terrace for a lesser-known city view, then cross to the leafy Jardim da Estrela opposite — a fine green pause with a duck pond and playground.

The city's oldest church, a fortress-like Romanesque bulk from the 12th century begun soon after Lisbon was taken from the Moors, with a Gothic ambulatory and cloister behind. It sits right on the Tram 28 route below the castle, an easy and dignified stop.

venues.n: Monastery of São Vicente de Fora
venues.d: A grand Mannerist monastery whose corridors hold one of Portugal's largest displays of blue-and-white azulejo panels, including whimsical La Fontaine fables, plus the royal pantheon of the Braganza dynasty. Climb to the rooftop for a superb, uncrowded view over Alfama and the river.

A vast domed Baroque church, centuries in the building, now the resting place of Portugal's great figures — including fado's Amália Rodrigues and footballer Eusébio. The rooftop terrace circling the dome gives one of the widest 360-degree views in the city, over Alfama's rooftops and the cruise port.

The highest of the city's viewpoints, where Lisbon's panorama feels most complete — the eye travels from the castle across the whole tumble of rooftops to the Tagus and the long line of the bridge. Less trafficked than the Alfama terraces; magical at sunset, so arrive a little early for a bench.

venues.n: Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara
venues.d: One of Lisbon's largest landscaped viewing terraces, its symmetrical box hedges and busts aligned directly across the valley to the floodlit castle. Reachable by the antique Glória funicular up from Avenida da Liberdade — a small, charming ride in itself — and lovely in the early evening.

Lisbon's oldest covered market, open since 1892, half of it reborn as a curated food hall where the city's best chefs run stalls under one roof — a painless way to graze across Portuguese cooking, with plenty of vegetarian and seafood choice for a mixed group. Busy at peak times; go early or mid-afternoon.

A 19th-century industrial complex under the 25 de Abril Bridge reborn as a creative precinct of design shops, bookstores, cafés and rooftop bars — including the much-photographed Ler Devagar bookshop with its flying-bicycle sculpture. Relaxed and stylish for an afternoon; the Sunday market adds vintage and artisan stalls.

Lisbon's most refined district, its garden shaded by a vast century-old cedar trained flat like a giant parasol, ringed by independent boutiques, antique dealers and concept stores. Embaixada, a neo-Moorish palace turned design gallery, showcases the best of Portuguese fashion, ceramics and leather — ideal for discreet, high-end shopping.

A serene 1930s 'cold greenhouse' of shaded walkways, ponds, waterfalls and sub-tropical planting tucked into an old basalt quarry — three linked houses of green calm just off Avenida da Liberdade. A gentle, cool escape that reliably delights children and grandparents alike.

The city's formal central park, a broad carpet of clipped box hedges rising uphill from the Marquês de Pombal roundabout to a belvedere that frames a clean sightline down Avenida da Liberdade to the river. A flat, easy stroll and a good orientation point at the top of the grand avenue.

Lisbon's grand tree-lined boulevard, mosaic-paved and modelled on the Champs-Élysées, home to the flagship luxury houses — Louis Vuitton, Prada, Gucci — and the city's best hotels. The natural address for a UHNI base, with fashion, fine dining and the theatres all within a walk.

A significant modern and contemporary art collection in the Belém Cultural Centre — Picasso, Warhol, Mondrian, Bacon and more — a strong pairing with a Belém monuments morning. (Note: the collection has been reorganising in recent years; confirm current status and location before visiting.)

Lisbon's centuries-old open-air 'thieves' market', spread beside São Vicente de Fora on Tuesdays and Saturdays — azulejo fragments, vintage silver, old prints and genuine bric-a-brac for the patient browser. Best in the morning; a colourful, local counterpoint to the boutiques.

venues.n: Cristo Rei (Sanctuary of Christ the King)
venues.d: A 1950s Christ statue on a tall pedestal above the river's south bank, inspired by Rio's, with a lift to a viewing platform that gives the definitive panorama back over the whole of Lisbon and the 25 de Abril Bridge. A short ferry-and-taxi trip that reframes the whole city.

The great red suspension bridge, sibling to San Francisco's, defines the Lisbon skyline; the Pilar 7 interpretive centre takes you inside a supporting pillar and up to a glass platform 80 metres above the water. A short, memorable stop with real drama for older children and teenagers.

One of the world's largest and most admired aquariums, built around a single vast ocean tank you circle over two levels, in the modern riverside quarter left from Expo '98. Reliably the highlight for families travelling with children — book a timed entry to avoid the queue.

venues.n: Parque das Nações & Telecabine cable car
venues.d: The sleek riverside district from Expo '98 — wide promenades, gardens, the Vasco da Gama tower and a gondola cable car gliding along the water past the Oceanário. Flat, pram-friendly and calm, a good half-day for a multi-generation group wanting space and modern comfort.

venues.n: Ajuda National Palace (Palácio Nacional da Ajuda)
venues.d: A neoclassical royal palace, the last official residence of Portugal's monarchy, whose staterooms drip with silk, porcelain and chandeliers — and which now displays the Portuguese Crown Jewels in a purpose-built treasury wing. Uphill from Belém and blissfully uncrowded compared with the coastal monuments.

The world's finest collection of gilded royal and papal ceremonial carriages, a jaw-dropping parade of Baroque coaches dripping with carved cherubs and gold leaf, in a bright modern hall in Belém. Compact, universally appealing and easily folded into a Belém morning.

venues.n: Sintra — Pena Palace & Quinta da Regaleira (day trip)
venues.d: A misty, forested hill town of romantic palaces: Pena, a riot of red, yellow and tilework on a crag, and Quinta da Regaleira, with its symbolic gardens and the spiralling 27-metre Initiation Well. Cool, magical and deservedly essential — a private driver-guide is the sane way to see two or three sites in a day.

An elegant former royal seaside resort of pastel villas, a pretty marina, sandy bays and the dramatic Boca do Inferno sea cave, easily reached by a scenic coastal train. A gentle, breezy counterpoint to city sightseeing, with good seafront dining for a relaxed lunch.

The westernmost point of continental Europe — a lighthouse on wild cliffs 140 metres above the Atlantic, where Portugal's poet Camões wrote that the land ends and the sea begins. A short, spectacular stop that pairs naturally with a Sintra or Cascais drive.

A perfectly preserved medieval walled town of whitewashed houses and bougainvillea, once a wedding gift to Portugal's queens, that you can circle atop its ramparts. Try the cherry liqueur 'ginjinha' served in a chocolate cup; charming and unhurried, and often combined with the coast at Nazaré.

A working port city famed for fresh fried cuttlefish and Moscatel wine, gateway to the Arrábida Natural Park — limestone cliffs plunging to turquoise coves like Galapinhos and Portinho da Arrábida, among the loveliest beaches in Portugal. Boat trips from Setúbal often spot the resident bottlenose dolphins.

Between Lisbon and Arrábida lie the historic José Maria da Fonseca cellars — makers of Portugal's celebrated Moscatel de Setúbal — and the villages behind the famous soft Azeitão sheep's cheese and hand-painted azulejo workshops. A refined tasting circuit that a concierge can arrange privately.

The great 18th-century aqueduct strides across the Alcântara valley on colossal stone arches — one of Europe's boldest — and its terminal reservoir, the cavernous Mãe d'Água cistern, can be visited as an atmospheric, echoing water chamber. A little-known feat of engineering away from the crowds.

The serene modernist gardens surrounding the Gulbenkian — lakes, sculpture and shade that locals treasure — wrap the Centro de Arte Moderna, home to the finest collection of 20th-century Portuguese art. A cultured, green half-day, recently reopened after a redesign of its grounds and galleries.

A landscaped waterfront promenade between Cais do Sodré and Praça do Comércio, with tiered steps down to the Tagus where the shipyards of the discoveries once stood — the best place in the centre to sit by the water at sunset. Flat, gentle and free, threading the two riverside squares together.
Lisbon's globally-ranked speakeasy — a hidden 'press to enter' door and one of the most inventive cocktail lists in Iberia.
Constança Cordeiro's tiny, sustainability-led bar — foraged, seasonal, locally-made drinks in an intimate den.
The refined rooftop of the Tivoli on the Liberdade — polished cocktails and an elevated sweep across the city.
A wooden terrace six floors above Praça Martim Moniz — a direct, dramatic view up to São Jorge Castle.
Lisbon's cult rooftop — a lush garden bar on top of a Bairro Alto car park, with the river and the Basílica da Estrela beyond.
A former bordello turned baroque, red-velvet bar on the old sailors' street — theatrical, decadent and quintessentially Lisbon.
A labyrinth of five rooms crammed with a century of curiosities — Lisbon's most famous, most eccentric old bar.
